w:r.w:t: Domestic services have existed for as long as human societies have formed households and social hierarchies. In early civilizations, domestic work was closely linked to systems of slavery and servitude. In ancient societies such as those of Egypt, Greece, and Rome, household tasks like cooking, cleaning, and childcare were typically performed by enslaved people or servants, and the presence of domestic workers was a clear sign of wealth and social status.

During the medieval period, domestic service became a common feature of everyday life, especially in feudal societies. Servants often lived with their employers and were considered part of the household rather than separate workers. Many young people entered domestic service temporarily as a way to gain food, shelter, skills, and social connections. At this time, domestic work was not viewed as a permanent occupation but as a stage in life before marriage or independent work. The early modern period saw domestic service expand further with urban growth and economic change. As towns and cities developed, more households employed servants, and domestic service became one of the largest forms of employment, particularly for women. Although servants increasingly received wages, relationships between employers and workers remained deeply unequal and shaped by rigid social hierarchies.

The Industrial Revolution brought major changes to labor and household life. While many workers moved into factories, domestic service continued to thrive, especially among the growing middle classes. Hiring domestic workers became a symbol of respectability, and domestic labor was more clearly defined as paid work. However, it remained poorly regulated, with long hours, low wages, and limited rights, and it continued to be dominated by women.

In the twentieth century, the demand for live-in domestic workers declined in many parts of the world due to labor reforms, expanded education, and the introduction of household technologies that reduced the need for manual labor. Nevertheless, domestic services did not disappear. Instead, they adapted, increasingly relying on part-time, informal, and migrant labor, often without adequate legal protection.

Today, domestic services remain essential to households across the globe, particularly in areas such as childcare, elder care, and housekeeping. Although there is growing recognition of domestic work as valuable and legitimate labor, it continues to reflect long-standing issues of inequality related to gender, class, and migration. The history of domestic services therefore
reveals both continuity and change, showing how essential household labor has evolved while remaining deeply connected to broader social and economic structures.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed how services are delivered across various industries. Domestic services—including cleaning, laundry, childcare, cooking, home repairs, and caregiving—remain essential to households but are still predominantly managed through informal, unstructured channels. This often results in inefficiencies such as unreliable service provision, lack of transparency, pricing inconsistencies, and challenges in matching service providers with clients who need specific skills.

Domestic services refer to a range of household-related activities carried out to support the daily functioning, comfort, and well-being of individuals or families within a home. These services include tasks such as cleaning, cooking, laundry, childcare, elder care, gardening, and basic household maintenance. Domestic services may be performed by paid domestic workers, either on a full-time, part-time, or casual basis, or by unpaid household members. Historically associated with servitude and gendered labor, domestic services remain essential in modern societies, particularly as families balance work and caregiving responsibilities. A Domestic Service Virtual Space is an integrated, software-driven system designed to support the coordination, administration, and financial management of domestic service transactions within a digitally mediated service ecosystem. Core functional modules of the platform include service discovery and matching, booking and scheduling, service provider profiling and verification, pricing and billing management, transaction processing, performance monitoring, and analytics-based reporting. When integrated with Paystack digital payment system, the platform facilitates secure, cashless financial transactions through online payments, bank transfers, and bank deposit tellers, ensuring end-to-end transaction traceability.

Digital payment systems have achieved widespread adoption due to their high transaction speed, operational convenience, transparency, and enhanced security infrastructure. Within the domestic services context, digital payments significantly reduce risks associated with cash-based transactions, including theft, misappropriation, and payment disputes. The system enables households to execute remote payments upon service fulfillment, while service providers and platform administrators gain real-time visibility into transaction status, payment confirmation, and revenue flows.

The integration of service management functionalities with digital payment infrastructure results in a centralized, interoperable platform in which service, financial, and user data are automatically synchronized upon transaction completion. This real-time data integration enhances accountability among platform participants, supports auditability, and improves operational efficiency through automated reconciliation and reporting processes. Furthermore, the availability of structured transactional data enables platform operators to implement data-driven decision-making related to service optimization, pricing strategies, demand forecasting, and workforce management.

The proposed system operationalizes these principles through a scalable, web-based architecture designed to accommodate increasing user demand, heterogeneous service types, and evolving regulatory requirements. By combining digital service coordination with secure financial processing, the platform establishes a robust technological foundation for efficiency, trust, and sustainability in the domestic services sector.

Web 3.0 refers to the next stage in the evolution of the internet, designed to move control away from centralized platforms and return it to users. Unlike today’s web, where data, identity, and digital interactions are largely owned and managed by large corporations, Web 3.0 is built on decentralized technologies that allow individuals to own their data, digital assets, and online identities directly. The heart of Web 3.0 is blockchain technology. A blockchain is a distributed ledger maintained by a network of computers rather than a single central authority. Every transaction recorded on a blockchain is transparent, verifiable, and extremely difficult to alter. This structure makes it possible for strangers to interact and exchange value over the internet without relying on intermediaries such as banks, payment processors, or platform operators.

To understand Web 3.0, it’s essential to first look at the previous phases of the internet’s evolution. While these phases overlap and influence one another, each is marked by distinct technological advancements and shifts in how we interact with the web.

Web 1.0, often referred to as the “static web,” was the internet in its infancy, from roughly the early 1990s to the early 2000s. During this time, websites were static pages that contained simple text and images. Interaction was limited to reading content, and websites were often designed by developers and businesses to present information in a one-way

back to those early days of the internet: GeoCities, AOL, or early versions of Yahoo and MSN. The web was a static, information-driven experience. The user could only consume content, not interact with it. Websites were like digital brochures—helpful but passive. This era of the internet was defined by limited interactivity, basic HTML pages, and centralized control by a few dominant companies.
Web 2.0: The Social Web (The Interactive and Collaborative Web)

In the early 2000s, the internet began to evolve into what we now call Web 2.0. This era is marked by the rise of social media platforms, user-generated content, and interactive web applications. The web became more dynamic, and users began to actively contribute content, making it far more interactive.

Web 2.0 introduced the concept of the “social web,” where platforms like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and later Instagram and TikTok, allowed users to share their thoughts, images, and videos with others. This created a highly collaborative environment, where the boundaries between producers and consumers of content became increasingly blurred.

E-commerce also flourished during the Web 2.0 era. Companies like Amazon, eBay, and Shopify revolutionized how goods and services were bought and sold online, creating massive online marketplaces. Google and other search engines became central to discovering information, and cloud computing allowed for a more distributed and scalable internet infrastructure.
all these advancements, Web 2.0 still had its limitations. The internet remained largely centralized, controlled by large corporations like Google,

Facebook, and Amazon, which dominated the online experience. These companies collected vast amounts of user data, which often raised concerns about privacy and control. Additionally, users were not truly in control of their data—companies owned the platforms and the information users shared.
Web 3.0: The Decentralized Web (The Future of the Internet)

Unlike its predecessors, Web 3.0 is not just an iteration of the internet; it is a complete rethinking of how the internet operates. Web 3.0 promises to move away from the centralized, corporate-controlled model of Web 2.0 and instead emphasize decentralization, user empowerment, and enhanced privacy.

Web 3.0 leverages a range of cutting-edge technologies—blockchain, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and decentralized networks—to create an internet that is more open, secure, and user-centric. It envisions a world where users have control over their own data, where online identities are decentralized, and where interactions are more seamless and personalized.

Web 3.0 is about decentralization, ownership, and privacy. This new version of the internet is designed to empower users rather than corporations, shifting the balance of power and enabling a more equitable online environment.
Web 3.0 is built on a few core principles and technologies that differentiate it from Web 2.0. Let’s explore some of these key features.

One of the most significant changes in Web 3.0 is the move toward decentralization. In Web 2.0, a small number of centralized entities control the majority of online services. Companies like Google, Facebook, and Amazon control vast amounts of user data and shape the online experience. Web 3.0 seeks to change this by decentralizing control over data, applications, and online experiences.

Blockchain technology is at the heart of this transformation. By using distributed ledgers, blockchain allows for decentralized applications (dApps) to operate without the need for a central authority. These dApps can run on peer-to-peer networks, where users can directly interact with each other, without relying on

shift to decentralization also means that users will have more control over their own data. Instead of corporations owning and monetizing user information, users will be able to store and manage their own data, giving them greater privacy and autonomy.

In Web 3.0, the concept of data ownership is redefined. In Web 2.0, most of our personal data is owned by corporations. Social media platforms, e-commerce sites, and search engines collect data about us to target ads and improve services. However, this data is often used in ways that benefit companies, not the

3.0 introduces the concept of personal data sovereignty, where users have full control over their data. By leveraging blockchain technology, individuals can securely store their data and share it only with those they trust. This allows for greater
privacy, transparency, and security. Users can also potentially monetize their data, creating new economic opportunities.

Another key feature of Web 3.0 is the use of smart contracts. Smart contracts are self-executing contracts with the terms of the agreement directly written into code. These contracts automatically execute when predefined conditions are met, eliminating the need for intermediaries such as lawyers or brokers.

Smart contracts are powered by blockchain technology and are crucial to the development of decentralized applications (dApps). They can be used in a variety of industries, from finance and real estate to supply chain management and gaming. By automating processes and removing middlemen, smart contracts can reduce costs, increase efficiency, and create new business models.
Web 3.0 will also see the integration of artificial intelligence (

and machine learning (ML) to create smarter, more personalized online experiences. These technologies allow for the analysis of vast amounts of data in real time, enabling the internet to understand user preferences, behaviors, and needs more

AI and ML, Web 3.0 applications can anticipate user actions and deliver personalized content, recommendations, and services. Whether it’s personalized newsfeeds, tailored product recommendations, or automated customer service, AI-powered systems will create a more intuitive and engaging internet experience.

Web 3.0 will also feature an evolution of search engines, enabled by the “semantic web.” In Web 2.0, search engines like Google rely on keyword-based algorithms to index and rank content. While these algorithms are effective, they often struggle to understand the true meaning behind a search

semantic web aims to improve this by allowing machines to understand the context and relationships between data. This would enable more accurate search results and richer interactions with digital content. Instead of simply matching keywords, the semantic web will enable more meaningful connections between information, making it easier for users to find exactly what they are looking for.
The Impact of Web 3.0 Across Industries

Web 3.0 has the potential to transform virtually every sector of society, from finance and healthcare to entertainment and governance. Below, we explore some of the industries that will be most impacted by this next generation of the internet.
The rise of Web 3.0 coincides with the rise of decentralized finance (DeFi). DeFi refers to financial services that are built on blockchain technology, offering users access to lending,
borrowing, trading, and other financial services without the need for traditional banks or financial

using smart contracts and decentralized platforms, DeFi allows users to have full control over their financial transactions and assets. This opens up new opportunities for individuals who may not have access to traditional banking services, particularly in developing countries.
Healthcare: Secure and Decentralized Health Data

In healthcare, Web 3.0 promises to revolutionize how patient data is managed. Instead of relying on centralized healthcare institutions to store sensitive medical records, blockchain technology could enable patients to control their health data securely. This would ensure that medical records are tamper-proof, while also giving patients more ownership over their health

, decentralized healthcare platforms could allow for more efficient and transparent clinical trials, better supply chain management for pharmaceuticals, and improved accessibility to medical services globally.

The entertainment industry is also being transformed by Web 3.0, particularly through the rise of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and tokenized content. Web 3.0 offers creators new ways to monetize their work through NFTs, allowing them to sell digital art, music, videos, and other forms of content directly to consumers, without intermediaries.

This shift could change the power dynamics of the entertainment industry, enabling smaller creators to reach audiences directly and retain more control over their intellectual property. The proliferation of decentralized platforms could also enable new forms of content distribution, changing the way we consume media.

Web 3.0 introduces the possibility of decentralized governance through decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). DAOs are organizations run by smart contracts, where decisions are made collectively by stakeholders rather than a centralized leadership.

In the context of Web 3.0, DAOs could enable more democratic, transparent, and inclusive forms of governance. Whether in the corporate world, political systems, or community organizations, DAOs could empower individuals to have a more direct say in how decisions are made, creating a more participatory and open system.

Phases of System Development Life cycle (SDLC)

The System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) consists of several interconnected phases that provide a structured framework for developing a system. These phases include Planning, Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Implementation, and Maintenance. Each phase plays a vital role in ensuring the system is successfully developed, with System Design being especially critical in shaping the final product.

The planning stage marks the beginning of the System Development Life Cycle and focuses on defining the purpose and scope of the proposed system. During this stage, organizations identify the problems to be solved, set project objectives, and determine the resources required for development. Feasibility studies are conducted to evaluate whether the project is technically achievable, economically viable, operationally practical, and feasible within the available time frame. Effective planning provides a clear direction for the project and reduces the risk of failure in later stages.

System analysis involves a detailed examination of the existing system and the identification of user requirements for the new system. At this stage, developers interact with stakeholders to understand their needs, expectations, and challenges. Various data collection techniques such as interviews, questionnaires, and observations are used to gather accurate information. The goal of system analysis is to define what the system should accomplish without considering how it will be implemented. The findings are
documented in a Software Requirements Specification, which serves as a foundation for system design.

The system design stage translates the requirements identified during analysis into a structured blueprint for system development. It specifies the system architecture, database structure, user interfaces, input and output designs, and security mechanisms. Design decisions are made to ensure the system is efficient, reliable, scalable, and user-friendly. This stage provides developers with a clear guide on how the system components will be constructed and integrated.

System development is the phase where the actual construction of the system takes place. Programmers write and compile source code based on the design specifications using appropriate programming languages and development tools. Individual modules are developed and integrated to form a complete system. Proper documentation is maintained to support debugging, future modifications, and system maintenance.

System testing is carried out to ensure that the developed system performs as expected and meets all specified requirements. This stage involves detecting and correcting errors, bugs, and inconsistencies in the system. Various testing techniques, including unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and user acceptance testing, are applied to verify functionality, performance, and security. Testing ensures that the system is reliable and ready for real-world use.

System deployment involves installing the tested system and making it available to end users. During this stage, data may be migrated from the old system, and users are trained on how to operate the new system effectively. Different changeover strategies such as direct, parallel, or phased implementation may be used depending on organizational needs. Deployment ensures a smooth transition from the old system to the new one.

System maintenance is the final stage of the SDLC and focuses on sustaining the system after deployment. It involves correcting errors that arise during operation, adapting the system to changing user requirements, enhancing performance, and improving security. Maintenance ensures that the system remains efficient, reliable, and relevant throughout its operational life.

The proposed Virtual Space for Domestic Services is designed as a centralized, web-based platform that facilitates seamless interaction between service seekers and domestic service providers. Its primary objective is to provide a reliable, secure, and user-centered environment for managing service requests, scheduling, payments, communication, and feedback. The system addresses the inefficiencies of traditional domestic service sourcing, such as informal arrangements, lack of trust, inconsistent service quality, and payment disputes.
The platform is intended for use by multiple stakeholders:

Users (Service Seekers): Individuals or households seeking domestic services such as cleaning, cooking, caregiving, plumbing, laundry, or maintenance. Users require timely access to verified service providers, transparent service pricing, and secure payment mechanisms.

Service Providers (Domestic Workers): Individuals or professionals offering domestic services. Providers require access to consistent job opportunities, secure payments, a mechanism to establish reputation, and tools to manage their service schedules.

System Administrator: The administrator oversees the platform’s operations, including user verification, dispute resolution, monitoring service delivery, and generating system reports. The administrator ensures system security, data integrity, and operational compliance.

External Payment Service Providers: These entities facilitate secure digital transactions, ensuring compliance with financial standards, processing payments accurately, and protecting user financial data.

The system is designed with a multi-layered architecture, incorporating a presentation layer, a business logic layer, and a data management layer. The presentation layer provides user interfaces for users, providers, and administrators. The business logic layer handles authentication, service matching, messaging, and payment processing. The data layer maintains records of users, service providers, requests, transactions, and feedback.

The system incorporates intelligent service matching algorithms that evaluate service providers based on skill relevance, availability, proximity, cost, and reputation. The workflow ensures that service requests are matched to the most suitable providers efficiently. Additionally, the platform integrates secure digital payment processing, real-time communication, and feedback mechanisms to enhance transparency, accountability, and user satisfaction.

Interviews are an essential qualitative research method used to obtain detailed and meaningful information from participants. When interviews involve diverse social groups such as housewives, working-class individuals, and bachelors, it is important to follow established interview principles to ensure that the data collected is valid, ethical, and reliable. The principle of purpose clarity emphasizes that the interviewer must have a clear understanding of the objectives of the interview before interacting with respondents. Every question asked should directly relate to the research problem and objectives. Participants should be informed about the purpose of the interview so they understand why their opinions are being sought. In the case of housewives, the interview purpose may focus on household responsibilities and service needs; for working-class individuals, it may center on work-life balance and time constraints; while for bachelors, it may relate to independent living and convenience-based service requirements.

: Housewives are appropriate respondents when the study involves domestic management and household services, working-class individuals are suitable when employment and income factors are relevant, and bachelors are appropriate when independent living patterns and personal service usage are being examined.
